Describe the governing arrangements provided by the Articles of Confederation. What were the main weaknesses of the document?

generated_text:
The Articles of Confederation (AoC) was the first written constitution of the United States. There were various governing arrangements provided by the AoC, but the most important was protecting the power or sovereignty of the states.  The state would not have ratified the AoC if the federal government did not guarantee the powers of the states. The AoC defined a federation of sovereign states with a national government having limited powers.  It specifically stated “This Constitution [of the United States] shall be binding on the parties thereto as an compact, although not as a contract.” The federal government could only implement actions which were explicitly granted to it by the state. Any powers not explicitly granted to the federal government were reserved to the states. This meant there was a delicate balance of power between the federal and State governments. The legislative branch under the AoC was the Congress, which consisted of two chambers; a Senate withtwo members from each state and a House of Representatives with proportional representation based on state population. To pass legislation, both the Senate and House had to agree and the President had to sign it. If the President vetoed the bill, Congress could override his veto with a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.  
While this sound balanced, there were several weaknesses under the AoC. First, there was no mechanism for removing an uncooperative President. Second, even passing a law required a supermajority in the Senate (2/3) and a majority in the House followed by the President’s signature. As such, minorities could easily block any legislation. Third, the AoC relied on the good faith implementation of laws by the President and states. Since it wasn’t a true contract between the states and the Federal government, there was nothing that compelled either the President or states to abide by the laws they passed. Fourth, while declared a “eternal” compact, there was no means to amend the AoC other than through consensus among all the states. ### Instruction:
What is mass spectrometry?

### Response:
generated_text:
Mass spectrometry (MS) is an analytical technique that is used to measure the masses of ionized particles. The results are presented as a mass spectrum, a plot of intensity as a function of the particle mass-to-charge ratio. Mass spectrometry is used in many different fields and is applied to pure samples as well as complex mixtures.

A mass spectrum is a type of plot of the ion signal as a function of the mass-to-charge ratio. These spectra are used to determine the elemental or isotopic signature of a sample, the masses of atoms and molecules, the identities and structures of molecules and other chemical compounds, and to monitor reactions and interacting forces between atoms, molecules, and solids.

In a typical MS procedure, a sample, which may be solid, liquid, or gaseous, is dried andionized, for example by bombarding it with a beam of electrons. This process converts some of the sample's neutral atoms and molecules into ions, which are then separated according to their mass-to-charge ratio. For example, if the samples consist entirely of one element, such as carbon, all the resulting ions will have the same charge but different masses, corresponding to the various isotopes of that element. If the samples contain more than one element, however, the ions arising from those elements can have both different charges and different masses.

The ions are then subjected to one or more accelerations, most commonly by electrostatic or magnetic fields, causing them to travel along slightly divergent paths; this method is called separation by kinetic energy. Finally, the ions are detected, usually by impacting a surface coated with a conductive material, such as gold, emitting electrons which can be counted by means of an electron multiplier. Alternatively, the ions may be detected directly by a quadrupole detector or a time-of-flight device.

Another useful technique when trying to influence others to take action involves mirroring . Physically match the posture and gestures of the person you are attempt to influence when you talk. When done correctly this technique creates a subconscious signal to the other party that you pay attention and care about what they are saying. This signals triggers people into responding to you more openly and genuinely interested in what you have to say. 
Finally it is often useful to remind yourself that not everyone responds in the same way to different techniques. Consequently it is important to tailor your approach to fit the personality and relationship you have with the person you are attempting to influence. In most cases the deeper your relationship with the person the more liberty you have to use Techniques that involve greater personal disclosure. Although it is generally riskier to reveal your intent to influence when you have a weak relationship with the person you are trying to persuade. Cats need to communicate with each other for bonding, and relating with each other; they need to collaborate, play, and share resources. When they communicate with people, they do so to get what they need or want, such as food, affection, or play.

Cats use a range of communication methods such as vocal, visual, tactile and olfactory. Cats mostly meow to communicate with people, rarely with other animals. Cat vocalizations have been categorized according to a range of characteristics. Originally suggested by Levenson in 1967, cat sounds are often divided into two main classes based on whether the sound is produced with the mouth closed (murmurs) or opened (meows). Murmurs include purring, trilling, and chattering. Meows can be further subdivided based on pitch and intensity. A third class of sounds—growls, snarls, hisses, spits, and turns—are made with the mouth partially open and are used largely in threat displays.

In 1972, Feldman and colleagues classified cat sounds according to the muscle groups involved in making them. This classification system, or taxonomy, has been adopted by many researchers and is still useful today. According to this system, vocalization sounds are divided into five major categories based on the muscles used to produce them: laryngeal, labial, incisal/canine, oral and pharyngeal. Sounds produced by moving the lips alone are called mewing sounds. Purring is made by vibrating the voice box and diaphragm simultaneously; unlike other sounds, purring is not audible to humans because the frequencies are below those which can be heard by the human ear. Structural biologists use a variety of experimental techniques, most notably X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance, and electron microscopy, but also single crystal diffraction, gel electrophoresis, fluorescence, and others. These techniques give rise to two- or three-dimensional images of biological molecules, which are then analyzedusing computer software to produce models of molecular structure and dynamics. Experimental data is frequently treated using methods of mathematical statistics, and structural biology has close connections with both applied mathematics and computational biology. The resulting molecular models are used in many fields, including drug design, understanding of disease mechanisms, and verification of biological pathways.

### Instruction:
What is comparative genomics?

### Response:
generated_text: The core of comparative genome analysis is the establishment of the correspondence between genes (orthology analysis) or other genomic features in different organisms. It is these intergenomic maps that make it possible to trace the evolutionary processes responsible for the divergence of two genomes. A multitude of evolutionary events acting at various organizational levels shape genome evolution.[13] At the lowest level, point mutations affect individual nucleotides. These may or may not lead to amino acid substitutions in proteins coded by the genome. At a higher level, large chromosomal segments undergo Duplication, Lateral Gene Transfer, Inversion, Transposition, Deletion and Insertion events. Ultimately, whole genomes are involved in hybridization, polyploidisation and endosymbiosis events. Many of these events have played a crucial role in the evolution of complex eukaryotic organisms from simple prokaryotes. Given the vast number of possible evolutional scenarios, it becomes clear that any automated system for the detection of homologous regions in genomes will fail if it attempts to identify every single matching subsequence. To overcome this problem, initial studies in comparative genomics relied on the identification of clusters of conserved proteins within genome sequences in order to establish a gene-to-gene mapping.[14][15] More recently, the development of high performance computing environments and new algorithmic approaches has allowed the direct comparison of entire genomes without clustering their contents first.[16] The latter is now regarded as the standard approach, as it provides a finer grained analysis and allows the detection of overlapping genes.

Bioinformatics is an interdisciplinary field dealing with the analysis of biological data through computational methods, particularly using techniques from computer science, mathematics and statistics to analyze biological data. In many countries, this has led to the creation of large institutes dedicated to bioinformatics analysis, often supporting both database construction and algorithm development.

The rise of next-generation sequencing technologies has had a huge impact on bioinformatics, as it has become possible to sequence entire genomes much faster and cheaper. This presents both opportunities and challenges; on one hand, it allows for more focused studies on smaller sets of sequences, potentially improving our understanding of the functionally relevant parts of a genome. On the other hand, the size of the sequenced data precludes most existing align ment programs from being feasibly applied, demanding new approaches both on algorithmic and implementation levels. Additionally, the sheer quantity of produced sequence data creates new problems in database management and youtility analysis. Another novelty arising from next-generation sequencing is the possibility of detecting structural variants, i.e. modifications to the position, orientation or number of copies of particular DNA segments. How does grain orientation effect the dimensional movement of wood?

Wood expands and shrinks depending on its moisture content.  The relative amount of change, expansion, or shrinkage differs for each of the three main grain directions.  Those directions are longitudinal, radial, and tangential.  Longitudinal is the direction a tree or its branches grow length-wise.  In most lumber, this is its length.  The change in this direction is very small.  That is why a wooden ruler can be used without changing its measurements when ambient moisture changes.  In almost all uses, longitudinal expansion and contraction are small enough not to concern themselves with.  

Radial and tangential expansion and contraction are significant and different enough that they affect planar dimensions of a piece of wood.  The relative amount of change in each direction is specific to the wood species.  Regardless of wood species, the change is greater in the tangential direction than in the radial direction.  The tangential direction is tangential to the growth rings in the wood while the radial direction is perpendicular to the growth rings.  Expansion in the tangential direction causes a piece of wood to warp.  Warpage depends on the initial dimension of the piece, the type and size of fasteners used, as well as the environment the wood is situated in.  Designing furniture with the expectation that wood will move over time is part of being a fine woodworker.  Aligning grain between joined pieces compensates forwood movement.  Woodworkers refer to a piece of wood as "stable" if it moves uniformly from end to end.  Not all wood species are stable.  Some woods, such as cherry, tend to move more in one direction than another.  This property can be exploited by orienting a piece such that the dimension that changes the least is the one used in joining.

A merchant bank was historically a bank dealing in commercial loans and investment. In modern British usage it is the same as an investment bank. Merchant banks were originally private partnerships which traded in commodities (merchandise). Historically, English merchant banking began in the late medieval period. The earliest business of merchant banks was to facilitate the purchase and sale of commodities for customers who did not wish to assume the risks of holding inventory. Merchant banks would buy or produce goods, store them, and sell them when the price went up. This made them some of the largest employers in England by the 18th century. By the 19th century, as railways and then telegraph communication networked Britain's major cities, London-based merchant banks could begin to provide finance for industrial production elsewhere in the country.

By the early 20th century, following the establishment of the national economies of Western Europe and the United States, the role of merchant banks had expanded to include financing industry and commerce. Few firms retained the word "merchant" in their titles; Barclays Bank PLC was typical in describing its business as "investment banking". Following a wave of bank consolidations in the 1990s, many old-line merchant banks either became divisions of larger financial groups (as in Italy and Spain) or merged with other Investment Banks (Merrill Lynch/Thomson Financial). In the U.S., following the passage of Glass–Steagall in 1933, retail banking was separated from investment banking, and the latter was performed exclusively by separate entities known as broker/dealers. That distinction was eliminated under pressure from theSEC in the 1980s, leading to the rise of "universal banks", i.e. firms performing both banking and investments services. After the collapse of Bear Stearns in 2008, all large universal banks in the US have been forced to divorce their investment banking operations from their depositary functions, effectively restoring the division first outlined in Glass–Steagall.

prompt:
Below is an instruction that describes a task. Write a response that appropriately completes the request.

### Instruction:
What is the effective interest rate (EIR)?

### Response:
generated_text:
The effective interest rate (EIR), effective annual interest rate, annual equivalent rate (AER) or simply effective rate is the percentage of interest on a loan or financial product if compound interest accumulates over a year during which no payments are made. It is the compound interest payable annually in arrears, based on the nominal interest rate. This contrasts with the simple interest rate, which is the interest paid without compounding.

The formula for calculating the effective interest rate assumes that interest is compounded at another interest rate within each compounding period. For loans and mortgages compounds annually, this is the same as the nominal interest rate. However, for compounding monthly, this results in an effective interest rate higher than the nominal interest rate.

For compound interests occurring more frequently than once per year, the effective interest rate is calculated using the following formula:
    EIR = ((1 + r/n)^n − 1) × 100
where:
r is the nominal interest rate / 100
n is the number of compounding periods per year
The use of effective interest rates allows comparison of loans with different compounding periods.

What are the main components of Apache Kafka?

generated_text:
Apache Kafka is a distributed system that is composed of several components. The main components of Apache Kafka are:
- Topics: A topic is a category or feed name to which producers can send messages and read by consumers. It’s append-only, so old values aren’t removed automatically. Retention is controlled by the log rollover strategy.
- Brokers: A Kafka cluster is comprised of one or more brokers that manage the storage of messages in topics and serve as intermediaries between producers and consumers. 
- Producers: Applications that produce data and publish it to one or more topics in a Kafka cluster. They control how events are assigned to partitions within a topic.
- Consumers: Applications that subscribe to one or more topics and consume published messages. The only metadata retained on a per-consumer basis is the offset or position of that consumer in a topic. This offset is controlled by the consumer.
- Partitions: Within each topic, messages are split across one or more partitions, which are order events within a specific range of sequence numbers. With a single consumer, you get exactly-once delivery if a consumer group is used; otherwise, it's at least once. When a producer needs to write to a topic with existing partitions, it appends to the end of the highest partition number plus one.
- Replication: Each broker has a copy of every other broker’s data, except for the leader broker. The leaders handle all writes and replicate them to followers. In the event of a failing broker, another broker can assume its role.

The meaning is the same but the second sentence contains an oxford comma which seems superfluous. This camp argument states all additional punctuation should be warranted.

Regardless of whether one supports or condemns the oxford comma, strong feelings on either side are evident. There are stylish guides and even a parody twitter account @OxfordComma_. ### Instruction:
What is heterosis?

### Response:
generated_text:
Heterosis, hybrid vigor, or outbreeding enhancement is the improved or increased function of any biological quality in a hybid offspring. An Offspring is heterotic if its traits are enhanced as a result of mixing the genetic contributions of its parents. Parents can be two plants, two animals, or two people. The term "hetero" comes from Greek and means different.  It is also known as hybrid vigor and outbreeding enhancement.

Major breeders have exploited this effect to produce high-yielding varieties of wheat, maize (corn), rice, and other crops. For example, wheat grown today yields six times more grain than it did when humans first started farming it 8,000 years ago. Most of this increase is due to heterosis. Maize grown in North America today yields 250 times more grain than it did when the Incas first tamed it some 7,000 years ago.

The mechanism by which heterotic offspring acquire enhanced trait values is not fully understood. One popular theory proposes that heterotic offspring benefit from having a mixed or 'new' phenotype resulting from multiple alleles at many loci. According to this theory, called overdominance, heterotic offspring would possess the most favorable allele at each relevant locus; i.e., they would be homozygous with respect to all beneficial alleles. Becker and Jordan (1963) performed a meta-analysis of 41 studies involving 31 plant species using five different methods designed to test the overdominance hypothesis and concluded that there was insufficient evidence to accept or reject the hypothesis. 

An alternative hypothesis proposed by Ford and Wilson (1957) suggests that heterotic offspring simply inherit and express dominant alleles at a higher frequency than would be expected under random mating. This suggested mechanism implies that heterotic offspring are not necessarily superior to their parents but rather are merely less inbred. Inbringding reduces the genetic diversity of a population and can lead to decreased fitness. Latter researchers have argued that heterosis occurs because of epistasis; that is, interaction among the numerous mutations present in heterotic offspring.

What is Remote Sensing?

Remote sensing is the acquisition of information about an object or phenomenon without making physical contact with the object, in contrast to in situ or on-site observation. The term can be applied broadly to any sensor system that gathers data about an object from a distance, but it is most often used to describe the collection of spatial data (such as photographs and satellite images) for the analysis of land covers and other geospatial applications. An alternative definition has been proposed by the American Geophysical Union ("Remote Sensing: Past, Present, and Future", 2004), which also includes "in situ" measurements "made at a distance using equipment that is operated from a distant location":

    In physics, remote sensing is defined as the detection and measurement of objects, properties, and phenomena from a distance by means of specialized sensors. This distinction between “in situ” and “remote” measures is important because many processes, while they may be observable at a distance, cannot be measured remotely. Examples include sampling structures of the lower atmosphere (temperature, humidity, etc.) or surface soil moisture and chemistry. Although “in situ” sampling of these variables is straightforward, their long-term temporal variation is frequently addressed only statistically due to the sparse distribution of measuring stations and the large sample area needed to obtain sufficient signal. Here, the possibility of non-intrusive, frequent, and dense sampling using satellite-borne instruments holds the promise of closing this gap.

In general, remote sensing involves the use of some type of probe or detector to collect data about an object from a distance. Common examples include the use of a telescope to view celestial objects or terrestrial objects too far away to inspect directly, or using radar to detect fluid ranges within the Earth's atmosphere. In fields such as earth science and planetary science, where direct inspection of landscapes and astronomical objects is impractical or dangerous, remote sensing is a vital tool; however, in fields such as astrophysics, where direct inspection of stars and galaxies is possible, remote sensing is not regarded as a key aspect ofthe field (although still useful for distant objects).

### Response:
generated_text:
One benefit of using the ReLU (short for rectified linear unit) activation function in neural networks is its efficiency in terms of computational resources. The ReLU function can be implemented as max(0, x), where x is the input to the activation function, and it contains no multiplications or additions other than the original inputs. In contrast, the sigmoid function uses an exponential operation which can be computationally expensive. 

In addition to efficiency, the ReLU function has better convergence properties than the sigmoid function when used in neural networks. Experiments have shown that networks using ReLU as the activation function converge much faster when trained with backpropagation. This is because the gradients of the ReLU function are non-zero for all positive inputs, while the sigmoid function approaches zero as the input gets large. The non-zeros gradient helps the optimization algorithm find better solutions faster. 

The shape of the ReLU function also provides some advantages in term of generalization ability compared to the sigmoid function. When used as an activation function in a fully connected layer of a neural network, the ReLU function introduces sparsity into the representation space of the network. That is, many of the weights in the network will tend toward zero over time during training. In other words, the network learns to activate certain neurons only when necessary. This sparse representation has been shown to provide better generalization ability than dense representations.

### Instruction:
What is the difference between the Scala Future onComplete and andThen functions?

### Response:
generated_text:
both `andThen` and `onComplete` allow you to observe the result of some future via a callback function. However, `andThen` can be chained, and unlike `onComplete`, it guarantees the order in which callbacks will be applied. In addition, the callback given to `andThen` may be a partial function, handling only a subset of outcomes (e.g., only failure or only success). Finally, the `andThen` callback is typically used for side effects, while `onComplete` may capture useful results.

Consider the following example using `andThen` and `map`:

```
def demoAndThen(fut: Future[Int]): Future[Int] = {
  fut.andThen({ case Success(value) => println(s"andThen1: $value") })
    .andThen({ case Failure(_) => println("andThen2: failure!")})
    .map { i ->
      println(s"demoAndThen: $i")
      i
    }
}
```

When `fut` successfully completes, "andthen1: ...", "andThen2: success!" will be printed in that order. Similarly, when `fut` fails, "andThen2: failure!" will be printed once.

The equivalent using `onComplete` and `map` would be:

```
def demoOnComplete(fut: Future[Int]): Future[Int] = {
  fut.onComplete{ t: Try[Int] => println(s"oncomplete1: $t") }
  fut.onComplete{(_, errorOpt: Option[Throwable]) => println(s"onComplete2: $errorOpt")]
  fut.map { i ->
    println(s"demoOnComplete: $i")
    i
  }
}
```

In this case, when `fut` succeeds, "onComplete1: Success(...)", "onComplete2: none" will be printed in some unspecified order. When `fut` failed, "onComplete2: Some(..." will be printed once.

Finally, note that `andThen` is not chainable inScala 2.10.x but was made chainable inScala

 Classified boards (also known as staggered boards) are divided into three separate classes (in equal proportion, to the extent possible), with members of each class serving three-year terms and only one class of directorsup for election in any year.

### Instruction:
What are the 5 most effective ways to convert a prospect to a customer?

### Response:
generated_text:
The journey from cold prospect to loyal customer is as tricky as the alchemy that transforms a stranger into a close personal friend. While there are a thousand possible paths, a handful of methods have proven consistently effective as triggers for moving prospects down the funnel toward purchase.

The first is Personal Referral. A referral from a trusted source carries enormous weight with a prospect. This can be any trustworthy person or organization that the prospect knows and respects; think of it like a "pre-sale." When a prospect hears a positive endorsement, they're much more likely to lower their guard and open up to receiving communications from your brand.

Second is the Mass Endorsement. Think of this like a "soft-sell." It's the phenomenon where you see a lot of people endorsing a product or service, and it makes you inclined to try it yourself because there seem to be a lot of happy users. Examples include school or work colleaguesendoring a new platform, or your entire social circle raving about a new restaurant.

The third is the RAS (Rapidly Assisting Sale). This happens when you get in front of a prospect just as they're becoming aware of a need and you provide exactly what they're looking for at the exact moment they're searching. Think of Uber during snowstorms, or Zoom after lockdowns lifted. When you satisfy a recently emerging need, your conversion odds go way up.

Fourth is the Free Trial/Demo. This works especially well if your prospect has a high degree of skepticism about your offering. By giving them a taste of your goods for free, you lower the risk associated with purchasing, and put them in a position to experience the benefits of owning your product. Note that this method works best when the barrier to trial is low -- think Amazon Prime trials vs. a month-long HBO subscription.

Last but not least is the Urgent Bonus. This converter depends less on the merits of your offering and more on the psychology of the buyer. The offer can take many forms -- discounts, scarcity, bonus items etc. -- but the idea is that that by combining a compelling incentive with rapid action, you create some outside impetuses for buying that help overcome the natural uncertainty and slowness associated with the purchasing process.

### Instruction:
What is a spatial network?

### Response:
generated_text:
A spatial or geometric graph, sometimes called a geographic network, is a graph in which the vertices and edges are spatially located. That is, the vertices and edges are associated with a location in some spatial environment (e.g., the earth's surface). Thus, the topology (the set of nodes and links and the incidence between them) and the geometry (the locations of the nodes and lines) are both important in defining a geometric graph. Geometric graphs may also be identified as spring, gravity, or force field models because they tend to exhibit attractive and repulsive forces among nearby elements.

Examples of geometric graphs include road and transit networks, power grids, social and interaction networks, communication and internetworks, water supply and Distribution Systems, forest fire control lines, watersheds, soils, groundwater flow, insect or animal colonization webs, vegetation canopy networks, neural networks, and ecosystems. In each case, the underlying science involves relationships among the biological, physical, chemical, and/or human components of the spatial environments in which we live. The main goal of constructing geometric graphs is usually to better understand the structural and functional characteristics of these complex systems for the purpose of management, conservation, and design.

Geometric graph theory is a fairly new branch of mathematics based on the work of Doyle, Ball, Brand and Launius beginning in the late 1980s. Classic graph theory , founded in the late 1800s by Augustus De Morgan, Franz Cauchy, and others, is concerned with objects without intrinsic structure; that is, its core theories (and their generalizations) are insensitive to small changes in the basic topological structure. In contrast, geometric graph theory emphasizes the importance of metric data (the spatial locations of vertices and edges) and intrinsic topology (the adjacency or proximity among vertices and the compatibility of edge sizes and shapes). This focus enables one to formulate precise mathematical statements about the behavior of geometric graphs, stating exactly how graph parameters such as vertex degree, connectivity, and clustering coefficient change as vertices or edges are added or deleted. It also allows us to compute exact bounds and approximations to classic graph theoretical indices for arbitrary geometric graph, where before only results for special classes of graphs could be obtained.

Genomics is an interdisciplinary field of biology focusing on the structure, function, evolution, mapping, and editing of genes and their products - proteins. In contrast to classical genetics, which seeks individual genes responsible for certain traits, genomics analyzes multiple genes within an genome in order to understand how they interact to influence traits and disorders. Techniques used in genomics include cDNA sequencing, whole genome amplification, gene expression analyses, structural and functional genomics, single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis, and mutation detection. Genes are contained in chromosomes within the nucleus of cells. In eukaryotes, including plants and animals, there is linear assocation of many smaller genetic units called nucleotides to make up a complete genomic sequence, known as DNA. This double stranded molecule contains the instructions, or blueprint, for all living things. Each unit of nucleotide includes one sugar, one phosphate group, and one of four possible bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, or thymine. The four bases are sometimes referred to as letters and abbreviated as A, G, C, T. The overall sequence of nucleotides in DNA is unique to each species, constituting its genetic code.

Genomics also involves the study of genetic variation within and between populations, using a variety of statistical techniques including population genetics and computational biology. Intra-population diversity is often measured by means of microsatellites, while inter-population divergence is estimated using fixed differences (often called "private alleles") and more generally by means of the FST statistic.[2] Both kinds of diversities can be analyzed using various softwares specifically developed for this purpose.[3][4] All these analyses aim at determining the amount of genomical differentiation between two considered populations. These amounts may be converted into effective numbers of breeding populations using an adaptation[5] of the classic formula of Wright's island model.

Here's a proof by contradiction that the square root of 2 is irrational. First, recall that irrational numbers are numbers that cannot be written as p / q for integers p and q. Assume for contradiction that the square root of 2 is rational, which would mean that sqrt(2) = p / q for some integers p and q. Further assume without loss of generality that this fraction is in reduced form, meaning that p and q share no common factors. We can make this assumption because any integer fraction can be written in such a reduced form, so the existence of any rational representation for sqrt(2) would imply the existences of one in reduced form. Now we square both sides of the above equation, yielding

2 = p^2 / q^2

for some integers p and q not sharing any common factors. Notice that the left hand side is even (since 2 is an even number), whereas the right hand side is either even or odd depending on the parity of q. Suppose without loss of generality that q is even. Then the right hand side is even, so the left hand side p^2 must also be even. This means that p must be even as well, otherwise p^2 would not be even. So p can be written as 2 * x for some integer x. Substituting this into the above equation, we get

2 * x ^ 2 = 2 * q ^ 2

Cancel out the 2's to get

x ^ 2 = q ^ 2

By assumption, the left hand side above is rational, which implies that the right hand side is rational as well. However the only rational squares are 0, 1, and some positive integer. Since 0 and 1 are obviously not equal to q^2, we must have that q is some positive integer greater than 1. But this contradicts our assumptions that q and p were both less than or equal to 1, hence our original assumption that sqrt(2) is rational was false. Therefore by contraposition, sqrt(2) is irrational.

An aurora, also commonly known as the polar lights, is a natural light display in Earth's sky, predominantly seen in high-latitude regions (around the Arctic and Antarctic). Auroras display dynamic patterns of brilliant lights that appear as curtains, rays, spirals, or dynamic flickers covering the entire sky.

Auroras are the result of disturbances in the magnetosphere caused by the solar wind. Major disturbances result from enhanced activity of the sun. These events cause changes in the magnetic field strength and its orientation. When the fields line up with the Earth’s magnetic poles, electrons accelerated by the lightning-like phenomena called electric fields can precipitate into the upper atmosphere (thermospheric glow). The resulting ionisation and excitation of atmospheric constituents emit light of varying colour and complexity.  The form, intensity, and location of auroras vary. They occur mainly in the high-latitude regions (between latitudes 50° and 78°) around the Earth's magnetic poles. Auroral activity displays great variation, even over relatively short periods of time.

The first documented mention of the northern lights comes from Chinese philosophers writing about an event observed on 24 February 24 BC. The Norwegian explorer and missionary Olaf Magnesson was one of the first to describe the aurora borealis in modern times on 13 November 1621. In 1749, French physicist Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Maire discovered that auroras were related to solar activity. This observation led him to propose the existence of "magnetic force[s] proceeding from the sun". His ideas would later inspire Swedish physicist Anders Angstrom to name the cells of the solar atmosphere "solar magnets". In 1896, English geologist Alfred Gabriel Coleman suggested that the aurora borealis might be explained by electricity arising from solar mountains and flowing down to Earth. It was not until the 20th century that scientists accepted that auroras were related to solar activity and charged particles accumulating in the Earth's magnetosphere.

Hash distribution: This is the default and most commonly used distribution pattern in Synapse Analytics DB. Round-robin distribution: This gives each worker thread a fixed range of rows to process, ensuring that every record is processed by at least one worker. Broadcast joined distribution: This works well for small joins between two tables that fit in memory on a single worker thread. It’s usually not recommended for largejoins as they may cause out-of-memory errors on the workers.

Localized hash distribution: This is a hybrid distribution Mode Suitable for both small and large tables. Range scan/query distribution: This distribution mode is specifically optimized for range scans and queries against fully distributed tables. It allows Synapse Analytics DB to efficiently handle range scans without needing to allocate too many threads or resources.

Despite all these evidences, the notion of parallel universes remains purely hypothetical and has not been proven scientifically. ### Instruction:
What is RTGS?

### Response:
generated_text:
Real-time gross settlement (RTGS) systems are specialist funds transfer systems where the transfer of money or securities takes place from one bank to any other bank on a "real-time" and on a "gross" basis. Settlement in "real time" means a payment transaction is not subjected to any waiting period, with transactions being settled as soon as they are processed. "Gross settlement" means the transaction is settled on a one-to-one basis, without bundling or netting with any other transaction. "Settlement" refers to the finalisation of a payment transaction through the appropriate bookkeeping entries in the accounts of two parties to the transaction. "Settlement system" is a subsystem of a payment system, and provides for the delivery versus payment (DVP) of funds between participants via a computerised network.

In a RTGS system, participating banks immediately settle payments when a transaction is processed. Since the processing of a transaction in such a system isFinal settlement occurs almost instantaneously upon completion of the transaction in the RTGS system. There is no risk of non-settlement, and hence the system is regarded as "settlement finality". Participation in the system is mandatory for all commercial banks, and it is used exclusively by banking institutions for their inter-bank transactions. Membership of the system is usually limited to banks and similar financial institutions, and although some systems permit individuals or companies to access the system indirectly via accounts held with a member institution, most systems do not allow non-banks to have direct access to the system. This helps to ensure that the system is resort-proof, i.e. that it will continue to function even during a national emergency or catastrophe.

The Hartnett/Euro1/TIPS network is an example of a RTGS system operating within the European Union. In the United States, the Federal Reserve Wire Network is the correspondent banking network for same day settling funds transfers among participant banks in the United States. The Fedwire Network handles approximately 375 million transactions per year with a value exceeding $2.6 trillion. The phrase "Real Time Gross Settlement" was coined by the Bank of England, which operates a system under the name CHAPS. Most major currencies have such a system.

Pan genomic analysis of genetic variability in a species provides a comprehensive view of all potential genes present within the species. In contrast to traditional genome sequencing, which focuses on one representative genome per species, pan genomics aims to identify and catalog all possible genes present within the population. This includes both core genes, which are found in every strain of the population, and dispensable or accessory genes, which may be present in some but not all strains. By taking into account the full repertoire of genes present in a species, pan genomics offers a more complete understanding of the genetic diversity and adaptive potential of a population.

Pan genomics involves two main steps: Initial assembly of many genomes and Subsequent merging of contigs from different assemblies. First, many genomes of the same species are assembled separately using various short read alignment tools such as Bowtie2, BWA, and SHRIMP. These softwares align the next-generation sequencing reads to a reference genome or to each other to produce assembly of individual genome. Then, depending on the species, there can be several types of merging of contigs between assemblies. For prokaryotes, software like MetaWRAP performs clustering of homologous sequences from different assemblies and then creates a new merged assembly. For eukaryotes, alignments of contigs from different assembles are first created using MAFFT and then merges together using i580 software.

Overall, pan genomic analysis provides a more comprehensive view of the genetic diversity and adaptation potential of a population, and can be used to identify novel genes, understand evolutionary processes, and predict functional proteins.

It then translates these virtual instructions ran by the program into instructions that can be run by the underlying system or hardware. As one of the major design goals of Java from its early beginnings was portability, this capability allows the code to be compiled only for the specifications of the Java Virtual Machine, with the guarantee that any valid Java program running on one VM will be able run on another VM without changes. ### Instruction:
What is the central limit theorem

### Input:
In probability theory, the central limit theorem (CLT) establishes that, in many situations, for identically distributed independent samples, the standardized sample mean tends towards the standard normal distribution even if the original variables themselves are not normally distributed.

The theorem is a key concept in probability theory because it implies that probabilistic and statistical methods that work for normal distributions can be applicable to many problems involving other types of distributions.

This theorem has seen many changes during the formal development of probability theory. Previous versions of the theorem date back to 1811, but in its modern general form, this fundamental result in probability theory was precisely stated as late as 1920,[1] thereby serving as a bridge between classical and modern probability theory.

### Response:
generated_text:
For example, suppose that a sample contains many observations, each observation being randomly generated in a way that does not depend on the values of the other observations, and that the arithmetic average of the observed values is computed. If this procedure is performed many times, the central limit theorem says that the probability distribution of the average will closely approximate a normal distribution.

The central limit theorem has different forms depending on whether the random variables are discrete or continuous. In the continuous case, the limiting distribution is the normal distribution. In the discrete case, the limit is the Gauss–Pearson distribution. The convergence is rapid in the sense that only a small number of terms are needed for a good approximation.

The earliest version of this theorem, that the normal Approximation to the Binomial distribution is correct, dates back to De Moivre.

Many variants of the central limit theorem have been proved under weaker assumptions than independence; in particular, uniformly integrable martingales converge in law to a normalized Brownian motion.

The autism spectrum, often referred to as just autism, autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or sometimes autism spectrum condition (ASC), identifies a loosely defined cluster of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by challenges in social interaction, verbal and nonverbal communication, and often repetitive behaviors and restricted interests. Other common features include unusual responses to sensory stimuli and a preference for sameness or unusual adherence to routines.
Autism is generally understood to be a spectrum disorder, as it can manifest differently in each person: any autistic individual is likely to show some, but not all, of the characteristics associated with it, and the person may exhibit them to varying degrees and frequencies.There is large variation in the support needs of autistic people, and some are nonspeaking, while others have proficient spoken language.

The term "autism spectrum" refers to a broad cluster of neurodevelopmental disorders that share some common symptoms, but can vary greatly in severity and which symptoms are present. Someone on the higher end of the spectrum might have difficulty making eye contact, understand social cues, and engage in repetitive behavior like hand flapping. Someone at the lower end might not experience these symptoms very severely, if at all. There's also a great deal of variation within each end of the spectrum.For example, someone on the higher end might have profoundly delayed spoken language, while someone at the lower end might have perfect speech but difficulties with pronoun reversal (he/she reversal).

Theautism spectrum includes conditions such as Asperger's syndrome and PDD-NOS (previously known as atypical autism), which were removed from the DSM-5 diagnostic manual in 2013. These conditions now fall under the umbrella of autism spectrum disorder (ASD).Some say this change should not have been made, as ability to speak does not negate the presence of severe social impairments that are characteristic of autism. Inhibitors bind specifically to enzymes with high affinity, much as a key fits into a lock, and prevent the enzyme from carrying out its function.

Some drugs known as medicinal inhibitors block an enzyme's catalysis of an essential reaction, thereby treating a disease. Conversely, the inhibition of vital enzymes in non-drug contexts may threaten human health, as in the case of viruses that utilize cellular enzymes essential for their replication but blocked by human inhibitors. A naturally occurring inhibitor of angiotensin‐converting enzyme (ACE) has been isolated and named omentin‐1. It is thought that this inhibitor protects the vascular endothelium lining from Ang II‐mediated detrimental effects.

Most enzymes from a single organism have only one or a few substrates, and each  substrate is processed by a specific active site on the enzyme. The site on the enzyme that binds the inhibitor may be the same one thatbinds the substrate, or it may be a different site, called allosteric regulation. If the binding site is not involved in catalysis, then the inhibitor is said to be competitive; if the binding sites overlap then the inhibition is considered to be non-competitive. Regardless of mechanisms, however, all enzyme inhibitors decrease the rate of the enzyme reaction by blocking the passage of substrate to the active site.

On the film it will appear as if the tire is rotating in the opposite direction to what actually happened.This is due to the sample rate being insufficient to capture the frequency of the signal (the frequency that the tires are spinning forwards) and the signal becoming indistinguishable from another signal (a frequency of the tires spinning backwards).

TheMonty Hall problem is a probability brain teaser based on the classic TV showborne, Monty, and his three doors. Initially there are three doors. Behind one of them is a car and behind the other two are goats. You pick one of the doors and win what’s behind it. Then the host opens one of the remaining doors and reveals a goat is behind it. The host now gives you the option to either switch from your chosen door to the remaining unopened door or to stick with your initial choice. What should you do?

The answer might surprise you. The correct strategy is to switch to the unopened door. The probability of winning can be calculated using simple equations involving probability mass functions for discrete random variables. However, intuitively the correct approach can be understood by considering the number ofgoats that must be behind at least one of the two remaining unopened doors at any point in time. Initially all three doors have an equal chance of hiding the car. When one goat is revealed, the car must still be behind one of the two remainingdoors. Thus the probability that the initially chosen door hid the car is reduced from 1/3 to 2/3. The remaining unopened door must therefore have a probability of 1/3of hiding the car, which is equivalent to saying that one of the two unopened doors must hide the car. The correct strategy is to switch to the unopened door with prob ability 1/3.

What is CRISPR?

CRISPR  (an acronym for clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) is a family of DNA sequences found in the genomes of prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria and archaea. These sequences are derived from DNA fragments of prevalent bacteriophages that had previously infected the prokaryote. They are used to detect and destroy DNA from similar bacteriophages during subsequent infections. Therefore, CRISPR provides a form of immunity against bacteriophages (or phages) i.e. viruses that infect prokaryotes.

The specificity of these sequence modifications is achieved through the use of enzymes called nucleases that bind to the CRISPR sequence and recognize complementary sequences in the target DNA. The most widely studied class of nuclease enzymes is known as CRISPR associated proteins or Cas proteins.

Given its ability to specifically modify DNA sequences, CRISPR technology has been repurposed for genome editing in eukaryotic species including plants, yeasts, mammalian cells, and microbial populations. Applications of CRISPR include basic biological research, development of biotechnological products, and treatment of diseases. In particular, the application of CRISPR-Cas9 to edit the genetic material of mammalian cells has enabled the generation of cell lines with model genetic alterations amenable for studying the function of specific genes. The use of CRISPR-Cas9 to generate genetically altered animals can be employed to study gene functions as well as develop models for human diseases and biomedical applications.

In February 2022, the journal Science selected CRISPR genome editing as one of the breakthroughs of the Year.

There are two main strategies for employing CRISPR for genome editing:
1. Harnessing the "natural" function of CRISPR to selectively cleave regions of the genome based on complimentarity between the Guide RNA and the target sequences
2. Using nuclear pore complexes to deliver pre-formed guide RNAs and Cas9 protein complexes directly to the nucleus of the cell, allowing for "engineered" genome editing

### Instruction:
What is connectomics?

### Response:
generated_text:
Connectomics is the production and study of connection maps (connectomes) between neurons in the brain, both at the microscopic level (in individual neuron cells; cellular connectomics) and at the macroscopic level (between areas of the nervous system; macrocopmatography). Although most nervous systems have the same general architecture – a central nervous system composed of a brain and spinal cord whose elements are neurons that are connected by synapses - they differ significantly in details of structural organization. Thus, there is interest in producing large numbers of neural tissue samples for both in vivo and ex vivo analysis. Techniques for preserving neural tissue during fixation and reconstruction are improving rapidly, so that entire organs such as brains can now be studied in high detail. While historically data collection was done using manually placed electrodes or diffeorphilic stains, modern techniques use highly automated approaches to reduce artifact introduction and increase throughput. Most commonly used technologies include light sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM), immunohistochemistry, and electron microscopy, particularly with serial sectioning. Reconstruction of connectomes from these data involves both increasingly sophisticated mathematical algorithms and, whenever possible, direct tracing by experts. The goal of this latter approach is to create an open database of all connectomes in the animal kingdom. A variety of resources already exist including those devoted solely to the connections within specific regions of the human brain, such as the primary visual cortex.

Generally speaking, there are two types of neural structure, white matter and gray matter. White matter consists of nerve fibers which connect different areas of the nervous system whereas gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies and their dendritic tree. Connections between neurons are made via axodendritic synapses where neurotransmitters are released across a synaptic cleft and activate ion channels on the dendrite of postsynaptic neurons. These ion channel activations lead to changes in the membrane potential of the postsynaptic neuron and thereby modulate action potential firing. Gray matter is typically eight times denser than white matter but accounts for less than half of total volume in the human brain.
